title: If you override `hashCode()` to always return a constant (e.g. 0 or 1), how does it impact a HashMap/HashSet (all entries in one bucket, O(n) lookups)?
shortTitle: If you override hashCode to always return a constant, how it impacts a HashMap or HashSet

s1_definition.profdef: Returning a constant from hashCode is technically legal because it does not violate the contract; equal objects still share a hashCode. However, it is pathological for performance, because a HashMap and HashSet use the hashCode to spread entries across buckets, and a constant forces every entry into the same single bucket. That bucket degenerates into one long chain, so operations that should be average constant time become linear, and lookups, inserts, and removes all scale with the number of entries, turning an O(1) structure into an O(n) one.
s1_definition.analogy: At the National Bank of India, hashCode is the drawer number that spreads documents evenly across a filing cabinet so any one can be found fast. Returning a constant is like assigning every single document to drawer zero. The cabinet still works and nothing is lost, but every search means pulling out the entire stuffed drawer and flipping through every document one by one. With a handful of accounts you barely notice; with a million accounts every lookup crawls, because you lost the whole benefit of having many drawers.
s1_definition.oneliner: A constant hashCode is legal but forces all entries into one bucket, degrading HashMap and HashSet operations from average O(1) to O(n) because every lookup scans one long chain.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Returning a constant from hashCode is technically legal because it does not violate the contract; equal objects still share a hashCode. However, it is pathological for performance, because a HashMap and HashSet use the hashCode to spread entries across buckets, and a constant forces every entry into the same single bucket. That bucket degenerates into one long chain, so operations that should be average constant time become linear, and lookups, inserts, and removes all scale with the number of entries, turning an O(1) structure into an O(n) one.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** At the National Bank of India, hashCode is the drawer number that spreads documents evenly across a filing cabinet so any one can be found fast. Returning a constant is like assigning every single document to drawer zero. The cabinet still works and nothing is lost, but every search means pulling out the entire stuffed drawer and flipping through every document one by one. With a handful of accounts you barely notice; with a million accounts every lookup crawls, because you lost the whole benefit of having many drawers.

**One line to remember:** A constant hashCode is legal but forces all entries into one bucket, degrading HashMap and HashSet operations from average O(1) to O(n) because every lookup scans one long chain.

sections.s2_technical:
A HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets. To place a key, it computes the key's hashCode, spreads the bits, and maps the result to a bucket index. With well-distributed hashCodes, entries scatter evenly, each bucket holds very few items, and get, put, and remove are average constant time because the map jumps to the right bucket and checks a tiny chain.

When hashCode returns a constant, every key maps to the same bucket index. All entries pile into one bucket, forming a single long chain. Now every operation must scan that chain comparing with equals, so get becomes linear in the number of entries, and put must scan the chain to check for an existing equal key before inserting, which is also linear. The same happens in a HashSet, which is backed by a HashMap.

```java
@Override public int hashCode() { return 1; } // LEGAL but every entry → one bucket
```

Modern HashMap has a partial safety net. When a single bucket's chain grows past a threshold, which is eight nodes, and the table is large enough, the chain is converted into a balanced tree, improving that bucket's lookups from linear to logarithmic. But this only helps when keys are mutually comparable, and even tree-ified, a single overloaded bucket is far worse than proper distribution. It is a mitigation, not a cure, and you should never rely on it.

The contract angle is important to state precisely. A constant hashCode does not break correctness: equal objects still return equal hashCodes, so lookups still find the right entry and sets still deduplicate. The damage is purely to performance. That is why it compiles, runs, passes small tests, and then collapses under production volume, which makes it a dangerous latent bug.

A senior point is that this is a real-world performance incident pattern: a developer returns a constant or uses a single low-cardinality field, tests pass with ten rows, and at a million rows the service times out because every map operation is scanning one giant chain. Another senior point is the fix is to build hashCode from the same distinguishing fields used in equals, usually with Objects.hash, so the codes spread keys across buckets and restore average constant-time behavior.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — An account class returned a constant hashCode, and a map of many accounts worked correctly but became slow as volume grew because all entries sat in one bucket. This is exactly the one-bucket performance collapse.

Problem 2 — Switching to a hashCode built from the account id spread entries across buckets and restored fast lookups. This is exactly the fix.

The code defines a `ConstantHashAccount` returning a constant and a `SpreadHashAccount` using Objects.hash, and a `ConstantHashCodeDemo` main class that fills a large map with each and times lookups to show the difference, while confirming correctness is unaffected.
sections.s4a_structure:
```
constant-hashcode-demo/
├── src/
│   └── main/java/com/bank/core/
│       ├── ConstantHashAccount.java   (hashCode returns 1 — all one bucket)
│       ├── SpreadHashAccount.java      (hashCode from id — spread evenly)
│       └── ConstantHashCodeDemo.java    (main — timing comparison)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Compile
javac -d out src/main/java/com/bank/core/*.java

# Run
java -cp out com.bank.core.ConstantHashCodeDemo
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is twenty thousand accounts inserted into two maps, one keyed by a constant-hashCode account and one by a spread-hashCode account, followed by twenty thousand lookups in each.

Step 1: The constant map inserts all twenty thousand accounts. Every key returns one as its hashCode, so every entry maps to the same single bucket, building one chain of twenty thousand nodes.

Step 2: Each lookup in the constant map jumps to that single bucket and then scans the long chain with equals until it finds the match, so each lookup does work proportional to the number of entries.

Step 3: The total time for the constant map is large and grows with the square of the entry count, which the demo reports in milliseconds, demonstrating the O(n) per lookup collapse.

Step 4: The spread map inserts the same accounts, but the hashCode derived from the account id distributes entries across many buckets, so each bucket holds very few nodes.

Step 5: Each lookup in the spread map jumps to the correct bucket and checks a tiny chain, so the total time is far smaller, demonstrating average constant-time behavior, while a spot check confirms correctness is identical for both.

```
Oct 30, 2026 ... WARNING: Constant hashCode: 20000 lookups took 4200 ms (O(n) per lookup)
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: Spread hashCode: 20000 lookups took 6 ms (O(1) per lookup)
Oct 30, 2026 ... INFO: Correctness check (spread) get SAV5 → 5
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  CONSTANT hashCode()=1
    put(SAV0..SAV19999) → ALL → bucket 1
      bucket 1: [SAV0]→[SAV1]→...→[SAV19999]   (one chain of 20000)
    get(SAVk) → scan whole chain with equals → O(n)

  SPREAD hashCode()=hash(id)
    put(SAV0..SAV19999) → distributed across ~many buckets
      bucket 7:[SAV12] bucket 88:[SAV5] ... (tiny chains)
    get(SAVk) → jump to its bucket → tiny scan → O(1) avg
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Bucket Distribution ═══

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ───────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: hashCode derives from the distinguishing field       │
  └──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌───────────────────────────┐   ┌───────────────────────────┐
  │   ConstantHashAccount      │   │    SpreadHashAccount       │
  │  + equals(Object)          │   │  + equals(Object)          │
  │  + hashCode() = 1          │   │  + hashCode() = hash(id)   │
  └───────────────────────────┘   └───────────────────────────┘
     all entries → 1 bucket           entries spread → many buckets
     O(n) ops (tree-ify helps a bit)  O(1) average

  Note: contract NOT violated by constant hashCode — only performance ruined.

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. fill constant map n=20000 → one chain
  2. n lookups → each scans chain → slow (O(n))
  3. fill spread map n=20000 → balanced
  4. n lookups → each tiny scan → fast (O(1) avg)
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Returning a constant from hashCode is technically legal, and it is important to say that first, because it does not break the contract: equal objects still return the same hashCode, so lookups still find the right entry and sets still deduplicate correctly. The damage is entirely to performance, which is exactly why it is such a dangerous latent bug.

A HashMap stores entries in an array of buckets and uses the hashCode to choose a bucket. With well-distributed codes, entries scatter evenly, each bucket holds a few items, and get, put, and remove are average constant time. When hashCode returns a constant, every key maps to the same bucket, all entries pile into one long chain, and every operation must scan that chain with equals. So get becomes linear in the number of entries, put becomes linear because it scans for an existing equal key, and a HashSet, which is backed by a HashMap, degrades the same way.

Modern HashMap has a partial safety net where a bucket whose chain grows past eight nodes is converted to a balanced tree, improving that bucket from linear to logarithmic, but that only works when the keys are mutually comparable, and even then one overloaded bucket is far worse than proper distribution. It is a mitigation, not a cure, and I never rely on it.

The reason this matters in practice is that it is a classic production incident: a developer returns a constant or hashes a single low-cardinality field, the tests pass with ten rows, and at a million rows the service times out because every map operation scans one giant chain. The fix is to build hashCode from the same distinguishing fields I use in equals, usually with Objects.hash of the account id, so the codes spread keys across buckets and restore average constant-time behavior. I demonstrated this by timing twenty thousand lookups: the constant version took seconds while the spread version took single-digit milliseconds, with identical correctness. So my complete answer is that a constant hashCode is legal but collapses a hash collection from O(1) to O(n) by funneling everything into one bucket, and the cure is a well-distributed hashCode from the identifying fields.
